table.caption: Smoothies buyers want each day at five prices (invented data for practice)

demand-s2.title: A year in Hollis's electric scooter market
demand-s2.text: Hollis is an invented city where many people rent electric scooters by the ride. Over one year: (1) the price of gasoline jumps, making car trips more expensive; (2) a new university campus opens, bringing 10,000 students to the city; (3) the scooter company announces that ride prices will drop sharply next month; (4) the scooter company raises its own price per ride from \$3 to \$4.

items.q: Buyers' incomes rise, and pizza is a normal good. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for pizza.

why.correct: For a normal good, higher incomes raise the quantity demanded at every price: demand shifts right.

key.because: a rise in buyers' incomes for a normal good

slips.S: Income belongs to buyers, so it shifts demand; it does not change pizza makers' costs.

items.q: The price of gasoline rises sharply. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for large, fuel-hungry SUVs.

why.correct: Gasoline and SUVs are complements. Dearer gas makes owning an SUV more costly, so fewer SUVs are wanted at every price: demand shifts left.

key.because: a rise in the price of gasoline, a complement

slips.S: Gasoline is used with SUVs by buyers, so its price shifts demand for SUVs, not the supply of SUVs.

items.q: The price of coffee rises. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for tea.

why.correct: Coffee and tea are substitutes. When coffee costs more, some buyers switch to tea: demand for tea shifts right.

key.because: a rise in the price of coffee, a substitute

slips.S: Coffee's price changes what tea buyers want, so it shifts the demand for tea.

items.q: The price of movie tickets falls and nothing else changes. Place point X where buyers end up on the demand curve.

why.correct: A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the demand curve: a lower price, a larger quantity demanded. The curve does not shift.

items.q: Incomes in a town rise, and for its residents store-brand instant noodles are an inferior good. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for these noodles.

why.correct: An inferior good is one buyers want less of as their incomes rise (they switch to pricier options), so demand shifts left.

key.because: a rise in incomes for an inferior good

slips.S: Income belongs to buyers, so it shifts demand, not the noodle makers' supply.

items.q: Which law does the table illustrate?
options: The law of demand: as price rises, demand shifts to the left
The law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls
A direct relationship between price and quantity demanded
A change in demand caused by a change in income

why.correct: Each \$1 rise in price comes with 20 fewer smoothies wanted, along one demand curve: the law of demand.
options: A price change moves along the curve; it does not shift demand.
Right: price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions: an inverse relationship.
Only the price changes in the table, so the curve itself does not move.

items.q: Using the table, by how many smoothies a day does the quantity demanded fall when the price rises from \$3 to \$5?

why.correct: At \$3 buyers want 80 and at \$5 they want 40: $80 - 40 = 40$ fewer smoothies a day.

mistakes.why: That is the change in price. The question asks for the change in the quantity demanded: 80 - 40.
You added the two quantities. A change is the difference: 80 - 40.

items.q: The stand raises its price from \$4 to \$5. How should you describe what happens?
options: Quantity demanded falls from 60 to 40, a movement along the demand curve
Demand decreases, so the demand curve shifts left
Demand increases, because the stand earns more per smoothie
Quantity demanded rises, because the price rose

why.correct: A change in the good's own price changes the quantity demanded, a movement along the curve, not demand itself.
options: Right: a movement along the curve, from 60 to 40.
Demand shifts only when something other than the smoothie price changes.
The stand's earnings do not change how many smoothies buyers want at each price.
The law of demand says quantity demanded falls as price rises.

items.q: A heat wave arrives, and at every price buyers now want 30 more smoothies a day than the table shows. What happened?
options: Quantity demanded increased along the same demand curve
Demand decreased: the curve shifted left
The law of demand stopped holding
Demand increased: the whole demand curve shifted right

why.correct: More wanted at every price, because of the weather, is a change in demand: a shift right.
options: A movement along the curve needs a change in the smoothie price.
More smoothies are wanted, so demand rose, not fell.
Price and quantity demanded still move in opposite directions on the new curve.
Right: a non-price change shifts demand right.

items.q: Event (1): gasoline prices jump. What happens to the demand for scooter rides in Hollis?
options: It decreases, because gasoline and scooter rides are complements for riders
The quantity demanded rises along the same curve
It increases, because scooter rides are a substitute for car trips
It does not change, because scooters do not use gasoline

why.correct: When car trips cost more, some riders switch to scooters, a substitute: demand for scooter rides shifts right.
options: Complements are used together; scooters replace car trips instead.
The scooter price did not change, so this is a shift, not a movement.
Right: a dearer substitute raises demand.
The link is through car trips, which compete with scooter rides.

items.q: Event (2): 10,000 students arrive. How does this affect the scooter market?
options: Demand decreases, because students have low incomes
Demand increases, because there are more buyers
Supply increases, because more scooters are needed
Quantity demanded rises because the price falls

why.correct: The number of buyers is a determinant of demand: more buyers shift demand right.
options: Even students with low incomes add riders the market did not have.
Right: more buyers, more rides wanted at every price.
The scenario is about riders, the buyers; it says nothing about scooter makers.
No price change is described for this event.

items.q: Event (3): riders learn that ride prices will drop sharply next month. What happens to demand for rides this month?
options: It decreases, because riders wait for the lower price
It increases, because riders expect a bargain
It is unchanged until the price of a ride actually falls
The quantity demanded rises along the curve

why.correct: Expectations are a determinant of demand. Expecting a lower price soon, buyers put off rides now: today's demand shifts left.
options: Right: buyers delay purchases until the price falls.
The bargain is next month, so buyers wait for it.
Expectations shift demand before the price changes.
The price has not changed yet, so there is no movement along the curve.

items.q: Event (4): the company raises its own ride price from \$3 to \$4. How does the graph of the scooter market show this?
options: A shift of the demand curve to the left
A shift of the demand curve to the right
A movement down along the demand curve to a larger quantity demanded
A movement up along the demand curve to a smaller quantity demanded

why.correct: The good's own price is on the vertical axis, so a higher price moves riders up along the same demand curve.
options: The ride price is on the axis, so it does not shift demand.
A higher price does not raise demand; it lowers the quantity demanded.
Down along the curve would be a lower price.
Right: a movement along the curve.

items.q: Why does the demand curve slope downward?
options: Sellers offer less at lower prices, so buyers buy less
Buyers' incomes rise whenever a price falls
A lower price lets buyers afford more (income effect) and makes the good cheaper than its alternatives (substitution effect)
A lower price attracts new sellers into the market

why.correct: Two effects explain the law of demand: a lower price raises buyers' purchasing power (income effect) and makes the good a better deal than substitutes (substitution effect).
options: Demand describes buyers; sellers' behavior is a separate curve.
A lower price raises what incomes can buy, but the incomes themselves do not change.
Right: the income and substitution effects.
Sellers are not part of the demand curve.

items.q: Which pair of goods are complements?
options: Butter and margarine
Hot dogs and hot dog buns
Train tickets and bus tickets
Paper books and e-books

why.correct: Complements are used together, so a higher price of one lowers demand for the other.
options: They replace each other: substitutes.
Right: they are bought and used together.
They replace each other: substitutes.
They replace each other: substitutes.

items.q: A student writes, "The price of pizza went up, so the demand for pizza fell." How should the sentence be fixed?
options: "The quantity demanded of pizza fell"; demand itself did not change
"The demand for pizza rose"; higher prices raise demand
"The supply of pizza fell"; prices affect sellers, not buyers
"Demand fell and quantity demanded rose"; both changed

why.correct: A change in the good's own price changes the quantity demanded (a movement along the curve). "Demand" means the whole curve.
options: Right: the price change is a movement along the curve.
A price rise lowers the quantity demanded; it does not raise demand.
Buyers respond to the price too; the sentence is about buyers.
Quantity demanded falls when price rises, and demand stays put.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: the price of coffee rises. Fill in each blank to explain what happens in the market for tea.

why.correct: Name the change, the link between the goods, and the direction of the shift.

specific.frame: Coffee's price ___, so some buyers switch to tea because the two are ___, and the demand for tea shifts ___.

change.label: Coffee's price
options: rises
falls

why.1: The scenario says the price of coffee rises.

because.label: How the goods relate
options: substitutes
complements

why.1: Complements are used together; tea replaces coffee, so they are substitutes.

direction.label: Which way demand shifts
options: right
left

why.1: More tea is wanted at every price, a shift right.

specific.model: The price of coffee rises, so some buyers switch to tea because the two are substitutes, and as a result the demand for tea increases: the demand curve shifts right.

items.q: Which events would shift the demand for gasoline-powered cars to the left? Select all that apply.
options: The price of gasoline rises
The price of gasoline-powered cars rises
Buyers' incomes rise, and these cars are a normal good
Many families move into the area

why.correct: Gasoline is a complement to these cars, so a dearer complement lowers demand for them. The other events either raise demand or move buyers along the curve.
options: Right: a dearer complement shifts demand left.
The cars' own price moves buyers along the demand curve; it does not shift it.
For a normal good, higher incomes shift demand right.
More buyers shift demand right.
